title: Sweep a chimney and deal with a chimney fire
summary: Look at the chimney and stovepipe often, and brush them clean whenever soot or creosote reaches 3 mm (⅛ in), which can be every few weeks with wet wood or an old or home-made stove. Creosote feeds chimney fires, which can reach about 1,100 °C (2,000 °F) and crack a chimney out of sight; the roof work is the other danger.

materials.item: Chimney brush the size and shape of the flue: wire for clay tile, plastic or stainless for a stainless chimney or liner
Rope and a cloth-wrapped weight, or screw-together brush rods long enough for the flue
Bright flashlight and a small mirror
Drop cloths or plastic sheet, wide tape, and bags or a bucket
materials.qty: enough to seal the stove or fireplace opening

materials.item: Fall-arrest harness and a tie-off point for roof work
Metal can with a lid for the sweepings
Dry-chemical (ABC) extinguisher and chimney-fire suppressant sticks kept by the stove

steps.text: Let the fire go right out and the stove cool, then take the ashes out in a lidded metal can and leave it outside: ashes hold live embers for days and give off CO (Drolet Part 1), and with the pipe off or the opening taped up that CO has nowhere to go but the room. Before you climb or lean a ladder on the chimney, make sure it is sound enough to take the weight (MU G1735).
steps.warn: A fall is the main danger. Ladder on firm level ground, tied or footed, 1 m above the edge, someone with you (CCOHS ladders). No wind, dark, or ice or snow on roof or rungs: in winter sweep from below (Alaska DOL snow).

steps.text: Look first. Shine a flashlight down from the top and use a mirror and flashlight from below, through the stove with the baffle out, the tee's cleanout cap or the fireplace damper (MU G1735, Drolet Part 1). Look for nests and blockages: a blocked flue puts smoke and CO into the house, so no fire until it is clear (NRCan wood heating).

Look where the deposit is thickest, usually the upper third (MU G1735), and scratch through it with a knife or screwdriver tip to see how deep it is (our tip). Under 3 mm (⅛ in) of dry soot can wait; 3 mm or more, or any shiny glaze, means sweep now (CSIA homeowner, Drolet Part 1, DuraVent DTC).

Seal the room side so soot can't blow in: tape a damp sheet over a fireplace opening, or take the stovepipe off the chimney and cover the hole (MU G1735). With the baffle out of a stove, keep the stove door shut while you brush.
Put on goggles, a dust mask or better, gloves and old clothes (MU G1735). Soot contains carcinogens and gets in through the skin too (NCI soot).
steps.warn: A damper plate that has seen years of heat can be brittle (MU G1735).

steps.text: Brush the full length of the flue, up and down, several times: on a rope with a cloth-wrapped weight on the other end to pull it back, working the rope from the top (MU G1735), or on screw-together brush rods if you have a kit (follow its instructions).
steps.warn: In a stainless chimney or liner use only a plastic or stainless brush: one that scratches the stainless must not be used (DuraVent DTC).

steps.text: No brush? A straw-stuffed sack or a length of chain pulled up and down on a rope will move some of it, but not all (MU G1735). Not in a stainless chimney or liner, which anything that scratches must stay out of (DuraVent DTC), and not in a flexible metal liner (AD J). Check with the light and repeat.
Take the stovepipe outside, bag one end and scrub each length with a long-handled brush (MU G1735). Replace any length with rust that has weakened it, especially at the joints (NRCan wood heating).

Clear the bottom: the cleanout door, the tee cap, the smoke shelf of a fireplace and the stove itself, with a shop vacuum if you have one (MU G1735, NRCan wood heating). Fallen creosote left at the bottom can block the flue (CSIA white paper).
steps.warn: Pieces of clay tile in the sweepings mean the liner is breaking up: check the chimney before the next fire (NRCan wood heating, AD J).

steps.text: Put it back: baffle in, cleanout shut tight (NRCan wood heating), pipe crimped ends toward the stove with three screws in every joint (NRCan wood heating), and the cap back on top (DuraVent DTC). See [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).

Relight with a small fire and the CO alarm working, and watch the pipe joints, the room and the chimney top for smoke (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1). If smoke spills into the room, put the fire out and open a window: a blocked or leaking flue, or a missing baffle, puts smoke and CO in the house or overheats the stove.
Bag the sweepings and keep them in a lidded metal can outside, away from the house: creosote is highly flammable (NRCan wood heating). Wash your skin and clothes.
Write down the date and how thick it was, and set the next check: weekly or monthly until you know your rate, at least every two months after that (DuraVent DTC, Drolet Part 1).

If you ever hear a roar or rumble in the chimney, see the pipe glow or smoke puff out of the stove: shout everyone out, close the stove door and air controls, and follow the chimney fire section in the notes (Drolet Part 1, CSIA preventing).
steps.warn: No water into the stove or onto a hot chimney fire: steam explosion in the stove (Drolet Part 1), cracked liner or warped metal in the chimney (MU G1735).

notes:
## How often to look, and when to sweep
Nobody can predict how fast creosote builds in a given chimney, so you find out by looking (Drolet Part 1). Chimney fires mostly happen because people are surprised by how quickly it built up (CMHC wood heat).

| Your set-up | How often to check | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Any stove, until you know your rate | Weekly at first (DuraVent); Drolet says monthly, and daily checks until experience shows | DuraVent DTC, Drolet Part 1 |
| Certified stove, dry wood, fires kept flaming | At least every two months in the season, and a full sweep at least once a year | Drolet Part 1, DuraVent DTC, CMHC wood heat |
| Old or uncertified stove, wet wood, or fires turned down to smoulder (a home-made stove: treat it the same, our judgement) | As often as every three weeks (NRCan) or every few weeks (CMHC) | NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat |
| Mild weather, spring and autumn, small slow fires | More often: Drolet says weekly cleaning may be needed in mild weather and monthly in the coldest months | Drolet Part 1, CMHC wood heat |

How fast it can go: with bad smouldering, NRCan says enough creosote to sustain a chimney fire can build in a few days, CMHC says a few weeks, and DuraVent says some stoves do it in two weeks (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat, DuraVent DTC). Older conventional stoves can't burn the wood as completely as certified ones, so they make creosote fast (CMHC wood heat): an untested barrel or other home-made stove is safest treated as one of them (our judgement). Never assume a chimney is clean (NRCan wood heating).

## The 3 mm (⅛ in) rule
- CSIA: sweep a masonry fireplace chimney at ⅛ in (3 mm) of sooty build-up, and sooner if there is any glaze; sweep factory-built fireplaces at any appreciable build-up (CSIA homeowner).
- Drolet and DuraVent: soot or creosote over 3 mm (⅛ in) means clean it now and look at how you're burning (Drolet Part 1, DuraVent DTC). CMHC rounds it to 4 mm (CMHC wood heat).
- Look where it's thickest. In a chimney that is usually the upper third (MU G1735). Scratch the deposit with a knife or screwdriver to see its depth.

## Reading what you find
| What you see | What it is | Will a brush shift it? |
|---|---|---|
| Dull dark dust or soft, dry, brown-black flakes | Soot and well-dried creosote, the kind a good fire leaves (CMHC wood heat, CSIA white paper) | Yes, easily (CSIA white paper, HETAS creosote) |
| Thick, shiny black flakes or crust | Heavier creosote, which sweeps call second degree (HETAS creosote) | Hard work; a brush may not be enough (HETAS creosote) |
| Black, shiny, tarry glaze, sometimes dripping | Glazed or "third-degree" creosote from smouldering fires, the most dangerous kind (NRCan wood heating, HETAS creosote) | No: brushing can't remove a hard or tacky glaze (CSIA homeowner) |
| Puffy, foamy, honeycombed deposit, very light, crumbles at a touch | What's left after a chimney fire (CSIA preventing, CSIA white paper) | It brushes out, but the chimney needs checking for damage first |

The degree names are a sweep's grading, not a standard. A crusty layer can hide glaze underneath, so look again after brushing (CSIA white paper).

## Brushes, rods, chains and sacks
- **Brush:** the best tool is a chimney brush the size and shape of the flue (MU G1735). Wire for clay tile; a plastic or stainless brush for a stainless chimney or liner, because a brush that scratches the stainless must not be used (DuraVent DTC).
- **From the top:** a brush on a rope with a cloth-wrapped weight under it, pulled up and down the flue (MU G1735). The rain cap comes off first; on DuraTech it's held by a collar screw (DuraVent DTC).
- **From the bottom:** through the stove with the baffle taken out, which Drolet says makes inspection and cleaning easier (Drolet Part 1); through the cleanout cap on the tee of an outside chimney (DuraVent DTC); or up a fireplace once the damper plate is out (MU G1735). This keeps you off the roof.
- **A sack or chain on a rope:** a burlap sack stuffed with straw, tyre chains or chicken wire pulled through the flue are the old substitutes. They don't scrape hard enough to get all the creosote (MU G1735), so use one only when there is no brush, then check with a light and do it again.
- **Rotary chains and chemicals:** sweeps spin a chain inside the flue for heavy glaze, and that can damage a clay liner (HETAS creosote). Powder treatments that make glaze brushable are a sweep's tool (CSIA homeowner), and chemical cleaners never replace sweeping (DuraVent DTC).

## Glaze you can't get off
Glaze left in a chimney is fuel for a chimney fire. Until it's gone, keep the flue gas in the normal range: DuraVent asks for about 150 to 260 °C (300 to 500 °F), and CSIA says flue gas above about 370 to 425 °C (700 to 800 °F) should be avoided because that is where creosote ignites (DuraVent DTC, CSIA white paper). A stack thermometer on the pipe about 450 mm (18 in) above the stove gives a reading (CMHC wood heat), but CMHC says thermometers vary and exact temperature figures can't be given, so treat the number as a guide. No overfiring, no armfuls of paper or kindling, and check weekly. Heavy glaze may mean a new liner, since getting it off can damage a clay one (HETAS creosote): see [Check a chimney](#guides/test_chimney).

## Staying safe while you sweep
- **The roof** is the dangerous part: see the [fall hazard card](#browse/hazards/fall). Sweeping is hard work, and the chimney must be sound enough not to fall when a ladder or your weight leans on it (MU G1735). In a Canadian winter, snow and ice hide vents and make the roof and the rungs slippery. A US state labour agency names falls as the top cause of death and injury in rooftop snow removal and advises methods that keep people off the roof where possible (Alaska DOL snow); the same sense applies here, so in winter sweep from below, through the stove or the cleanout, and leave the top for a dry, still day. A ladder is tied at the top or footed, reaches 1 m (3 ft) above the edge, and you keep three points of contact and carry nothing in your hands (CCOHS ladders).
- **Soot** contains carcinogens and gets in by breathing, swallowing and through the skin; chimney sweeps likely have the highest occupational exposure to soot (NCI soot). Goggles, a dust mask or better, gloves and old clothes (MU G1735), then wash.
- **Old fireplace damper plates** can be brittle from years of heat (MU G1735).
- **The sweepings** are creosote, which burns well (NRCan wood heating): bag them and keep them in a lidded metal can outside, away from the house.

## Burn so there's less to sweep
Dry wood, fires that stay flaming, no load left to smoulder for hours (CMHC wood heat, DuraVent DTC), and no big loads of paper or kindling, which people often report burning just before a chimney fire (CSIA white paper). See [What to burn](#guides/reference_what_to_burn), [Firewood](#guides/skill_firewood) and the overnight fire in [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm).

## Chimney fire: what it looks and sounds like
- Loud cracking and popping, a low rumble like a freight train or a low plane, lots of dense smoke, an intense hot smell, flames or thick smoke from the chimney top (CSIA preventing).
- A roar of air being sucked into the stove, a stovepipe that shakes or glows red, smoke and flame puffing back out of the stove, and steam from cracks in the chimney (CSIA white paper).
- Masonry chimney fires reach about 1,100 °C (2,000 °F), enough to melt mortar, crack tiles and collapse liners (CSIA preventing).
- Most go unnoticed: slow fires are quiet but still hot enough to damage the chimney and the wood around it (CSIA preventing).

## Chimney fire: what to do, alone
1. **Shout everyone out** of the house, and call the fire service if there is one (Drolet Part 1, CSIA preventing).
2. **Shut off its air:** close the stove door and air controls (Drolet Part 1, DuraVent DTC). This usually stops the flames but not the fire: creosote can keep glowing for hours and creep up the whole chimney (CSIA white paper).
3. **Chimney-fire suppressant** if you have it: the flare kind is lit and tossed into the firebox and uses up the oxygen in the flue; another kind needs no lighting: the sealed pack is thrown onto the burning fire (Kidde's FireEx). Kidde's advice is to cut drafts by shutting the stove or insert doors, or covering a fireplace opening with fire-retardant material (FireRescue1). Follow the packet.
4. **Otherwise** a dry-chemical extinguisher, baking soda or sand on the fire in the stove (Drolet Part 1); some of the extinguisher powder goes up the chimney and helps (MU G1735).
5. **Don't open the door or cleanout to look:** people who thought it was out have opened them and brought it back (CSIA white paper).
6. **No water** into the stove or onto a very hot chimney fire. Drolet says water on the stove fire can cause a dangerous steam explosion (Drolet Part 1); Missouri Extension says the rapid cooling can crack the tile liner or warp the metal (MU G1735).
7. **Watch for hours:** feel and look at the walls, ceilings and attic wherever the chimney passes, and the roof around it (CSIA white paper). If fire gets into the house, get out and stay out. More in [When no help is coming](#ref/reference_fire_heat/when_no_help_is_coming).

## After a chimney fire
Don't light it again until it has been swept and checked (Drolet Part 1, CSIA after-fire, NRCan wood heating). Signs of a fire, and of damage: puffy or honeycombed creosote; a warped damper, connector pipe or metal chimney; cracked or collapsed flue tiles or big pieces missing; a discoloured or bent rain cap; creosote flakes on the roof or ground; scorched roofing; cracks in the outside masonry; smoke coming through mortar joints (CSIA preventing). In a metal chimney look for separated joints, warping, buckling and open seams (CSIA after-fire). Much of the damage is out of sight (CSIA after-fire), so do the full check in [Check a chimney](#guides/test_chimney). A chimney fire also means something is wrong with the stove, the fuel or how it's burned: change it (NRCan wood heating).
